plan: Ten new items aimed at the hard end: two rare-word items with familiar-meaning traps, a difference-of-differences data item and "one of those who" agreement; no resubmissions pending.

passages.title: A careful historian
passages.text: Reviewers noted that the historian's account of the expedition's failure is deliberately ______: she meticulously lays out the evidence for each competing explanation but never indicates which one she finds most convincing.

passages.title: Late poems
passages.text: Although the poet's early work was widely imitated, her later poems were so ______ that few readers, let alone imitators, could follow their dense allusions to obscure medieval texts.

passages.title: Teaching methods
passages.text:
A district compared average test scores of students taught with two reading methods at urban and rural schools.
School type | Method A | Method B
Urban | 72 | 75
Rural | 64 | 73
A researcher claims that Method B's advantage over Method A was greater at rural schools than at urban schools.

passages.title: Caffeinated nectar
passages.text: Some flowering plants produce small amounts of caffeine in their nectar, which might seem likely to deter pollinators, since caffeine tastes bitter. In experiments, however, bees that fed on nectar containing low doses of caffeine were more likely to remember and return to the scent of that flower than bees fed on nectar without caffeine. This suggests that, for the plants, caffeine in nectar may ______

passages.title: Brooding octopus
passages.text: Dr. Imani Osei is one of the few marine biologists who ______ observed a deep-sea octopus brooding its eggs in the wild, a process that in some species can last more than four years.

passages.title: The treaty debate
passages.text: Historians have long argued ______ the treaty's harsh terms, rather than any single political leader, made the war that followed nearly inevitable.

passages.title: Sensitive periods
passages.text: In the 1950s, researchers found that some songbirds learn their songs by imitating adult birds during a sensitive period early in life; birds that hear no adult song then never sing normally. ______ human infants appear to learn the sounds of their native language most easily within their first year.

passages.title: Hummingbird notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Most hummingbirds weigh less than 6 grams.
• Scientists once doubted that birds so small could store enough fat to fly long distances.
• Rufous hummingbirds migrate up to about 6,000 kilometers between Alaska and Mexico.
• Researchers track hummingbirds by attaching tiny numbered bands to their legs.

passages.title: The cello
passages.text:
The following text is adapted from a short story.
For weeks Ana's scales sounded like a door creaking in the wind. She practiced them anyway, every evening, while her brother complained through the wall. Then one night in March she played the C major scale and stopped halfway, startled. The note had not creaked. It had simply rung, clear and round, and for a moment she was afraid to play the next one in case it would not.

passages.title: Bike lanes and injuries
passages.text:
Text 1
Many urban planners credit networks of protected bike lanes with reducing traffic injuries. They point to several cities where reported injuries fell sharply in the years after extensive lane networks were built.
Text 2
A transportation economist observes that the cities that built extensive bike lanes also lowered their speed limits during those same years. Lower speed limits on their own, she notes, have been linked to large drops in traffic injuries.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: never indicates which one she finds most convincing
candidates.explanation: An account that presents every side but declines to state a preference is "noncommittal."

A.rationale: "Ambivalent" means torn between feelings; the text says she withholds her view, not that she is conflicted.

B.rationale: Someone indifferent would not "meticulously" lay out the evidence.

D.rationale: A partisan account would favor one explanation, the opposite of what is described.

hints: Does the historian lack an opinion, feel torn, or simply not state her view?
candidates.remember: Distinguish withholding a view from feeling torn about it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: dense allusions to obscure medieval texts
candidates.explanation: Poems full of allusions to obscure texts are hard to understand: "recondite."

A.rationale: "Derivative" means imitative of others, but the text says her later poems were hard to follow, not borrowed.

B.rationale: Accessible poems would be easy to follow, the opposite of what is described.

C.rationale: "Prolific" describes a writer who produces a great deal, not poems that are hard to understand.

hints: What made the later poems hard to follow?
candidates.remember: Use the clause after "that" to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?

choices.A: At rural schools Method B students outscored Method A students by 9 points, compared with 3 points at urban schools.
choices.B: Students taught with Method B scored higher at urban schools, averaging 75, than at rural schools, averaging 73.
choices.C: At both urban and rural schools, students taught with Method B outscored students taught with Method A on average.
choices.D: Rural students taught with Method A had the lowest average score of any group in the district, at 64.

candidates.evidence: Method B's advantage over Method A was greater at rural schools than at urban schools
candidates.explanation: The claim compares two gaps: rural 73 - 64 = 9 versus urban 75 - 72 = 3. Only A states both.

B.rationale: This compares Method B across school types, not Method B's advantage over Method A.

C.rationale: This shows an advantage at both, but not that it was greater at rural schools.

D.rationale: One group's score does not compare the size of the advantage at the two school types.

hints: The claim is about a difference between two differences.

strategy.explanation: Compute each school type's gap first.

candidates.remember: When a claim compares advantages, compare the gaps, not the raw scores.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: protect the nectar from being consumed by bees, which would otherwise take too much of it.
choices.B: encourage pollinators to make repeat visits, raising the chance that the flowers are pollinated.
choices.C: have no lasting effect on how bees behave once they have finished feeding on the nectar.
choices.D: make the flowers taste too bitter for most bees, steering pollinators toward other species.

candidates.evidence: were more likely to remember and return to the scent of that flower
candidates.explanation: Bees given caffeinated nectar were more likely to come back to that flower, so the caffeine may benefit the plant by bringing pollinators back.

A.rationale: The bees still fed on the caffeinated nectar and returned for more, so it did not keep them away.

C.rationale: Bees fed caffeine were more likely to return later, which is a lasting effect.

D.rationale: The text says bees returned more often, the opposite of being steered away.

hints: What did the bees fed caffeine do differently?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that contradict the experiment.

candidates.remember: Follow the evidence after "however": it overturns the expectation.

candidates.subskill: Agreement in a "one of those who" clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: one of the few marine biologists who
candidates.explanation: In "one of the few marine biologists who ...," the pronoun "who" refers to the plural "biologists" (she is one of a group that has done this), so the verb is "have."

B.rationale: "Who" refers to "marine biologists," not to "one," so the verb must be plural.

C.rationale: "Having" leaves the relative clause without a finite verb.

D.rationale: "Is having observed" is not a standard verb form.

hints: What noun does "who" refer to: "one" or "biologists"?
candidates.remember: In "one of the ___ who ...," the verb agrees with the plural group.

candidates.subskill: No punctuation between a verb and its that-clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "That the treaty's harsh terms ... made the war nearly inevitable" is the object of "argued," so no punctuation separates them.

A.rationale: A comma should not separate the verb "argued" from the clause that is its object.

C.rationale: A comma after "that" splits the clause's subject, "the treaty's harsh terms," from its own conjunction.

D.rationale: A colon cannot come between a verb and its object.

hints: What does "argued" need to be followed by?

strategy.explanation: Remove punctuation between a verb and its object.

candidates.remember: No punctuation between a verb and the clause it introduces.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: learn their songs by imitating adult birds during a sensitive period early in life
candidates.explanation: Both songbirds and human infants learn their sounds most easily early in life, so the second sentence presents a parallel: "Similarly."

A.rationale: Human infants also learn best early in life, which parallels the songbirds rather than contrasting with them.

B.rationale: The songbird finding did not cause infants to learn language early.

D.rationale: Human infants are not an example of songbirds.

hints: Are the songbirds and the infants alike or different here?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the rufous hummingbird's migration surprised scientists. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Rufous hummingbirds migrate up to about 6,000 kilometers each year, traveling between breeding grounds in Alaska and Mexico.
choices.B: Most hummingbirds weigh less than 6 grams, which places them among the smallest of all the world's birds.
choices.C: Researchers who study hummingbird migration track the birds by attaching tiny numbered bands to their legs.
choices.D: Scientists doubted that birds under 6 grams could store fat for long flights, yet rufous hummingbirds fly up to 6,000 kilometers.

candidates.evidence: Scientists once doubted that birds so small could store enough fat to fly long distances.
candidates.explanation: A surprise needs both the expectation (small birds could not store enough fat) and the result that defied it (6,000-kilometer migrations). Only D combines them.

A.rationale: This states the distance but not why it was surprising.

B.rationale: This gives the weight but not the migration that surprised scientists.

C.rationale: Tracking methods do not explain the surprise.

hints: What two pieces of information make something surprising?

strategy.explanation: Name the goal, then check each choice against it.

candidates.remember: To show a surprise, pair the expectation with what contradicted it.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It reveals that Ana has decided to stop practicing scales after so many weeks of frustration.
choices.B: It conveys Ana's surprise at her sudden progress along with her fear that it may not last.
choices.C: It explains why Ana's brother had complained so often about the sound of her evening practice.
choices.D: It describes the moment when Ana first learned how to read the notes of the C major scale.

candidates.evidence: for a moment she was afraid to play the next one in case it would not
candidates.explanation: The last sentence describes the clear note that marks her progress and her hesitation to play on in case the change does not last.

A.rationale: Ana pauses out of fear the next note will not ring; nothing suggests she quits.

C.rationale: The brother's complaints are explained by the creaking scales earlier, not by the last sentence.

D.rationale: The sentence is about how the note sounded, not about learning to read music.

hints: What does Ana feel in the final sentence?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices the text does not support.

candidates.remember: Function questions ask what a sentence does in the whole text.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the economist in Text 2 most likely respond to the planners' claim in Text 1?

choices.A: She would argue that reported traffic injuries actually rose in the cities after the bike lanes were built.
choices.B: She would agree that protected bike lanes were clearly the main reason that traffic injuries declined.
choices.C: She would claim that lowering speed limits has little or no effect on the number of traffic injuries.
choices.D: She would suggest that the drop in injuries may be partly due to a different change made at the same time.

candidates.evidence: also lowered their speed limits during those same years
candidates.explanation: Text 2 points to a confounding change (lower speed limits) that could also explain the decline, so the economist would question attributing it to bike lanes alone.

A.rationale: She does not dispute that injuries fell; she questions the cause.

B.rationale: Pointing to lower speed limits casts doubt on bike lanes as the main reason.

C.rationale: She says lower speed limits have been linked to large drops in injuries.

hints: Does Text 2 dispute the data or the explanation?

strategy.explanation: Identify Text 2's concern before reading choices.

candidates.remember: A simultaneous change offers an alternative explanation for a trend.
